memo.intro: First-look memo as of 2026-11-01. Public data only. Every factual sentence links to its source; a separate verifier removed unsupported claims.

sentences.text: Setuav is tagged as a defense company, and the evidence consists only of GitHub activity for three public repositories.
Setuav/PyThrust is described as an open-source framework for electric propulsion system analysis and optimization in UAV design, with 153 stars and 23 forks as of 2026-11-02.
sentences.note: Description, 153 stars, 23 forks and fetch date 2026-11-02 all match source 65.

sentences.text: Setuav/Studio is described as a plugin-based desktop application for parametric UAV design and analysis, with 4 stars and 0 forks as of 2026-11-02.
sentences.note: Studio description, 4 stars, 0 forks and fetch date match source 65.

sentences.text: Setuav/mavlink2grpc is described as a schema-first MAVLink to gRPC bridge and code generator, with 31 stars and 5 forks as of 2026-11-02.
sentences.note: Description, 31 stars, 5 forks and fetch date match source 24.

sentences.text: The evidence shows no revenue, customers, funding, or defense contracts.
The evidence does not identify any team members.
PyThrust lists the topics openmdao, optimization, propulsion and scipy, and its repository has tests for autotune, battery, models, motors, openmdao, propellers and solver.
sentences.note: Topics in source 65 and test files for all seven named areas in source 316.

sentences.text: Studio lists the topics aerodynamics, aerosandbox, parametric-design, propulsion and weight-balance, and its file tree includes a plugin SDK package and an example plugin.
sentences.note: Topics match source 65; packages/setuav-studio-sdk and packages/example-plugin appear in source 330.

sentences.text: mavlink2grpc lists the topics ardupilot, px4, mavlink, grpc and protobuf, and its file tree has Node and Python client directories and a generator directory.
sentences.note: Topics match source 24; clients/node, clients/python and generator paths appear in source 322.

sentences.text: What looks novel is the stack as a whole: design tools, a propulsion optimizer, and a flight-link bridge.
Each piece is built on existing open tools, so the novelty is in integration rather than in a new physical method.
The hard parts are model accuracy against real motors, propellers and batteries, and keeping a plugin ecosystem coherent.
The file trees show no hardware-adjacent files in PyThrust or Studio, so validation against hardware is not visible.
The main technical risk is that the tools are accurate only on paper and give no edge over free alternatives.
The evidence contains no market sizing, customer, or procurement information.
A plausible reading is that small UAV builders need open, scriptable design and integration tools, and that defense interest in low-cost drones raises demand.
The evidence does not support this directly.

sentences.note: Six release dates match source 314 exactly.

sentences.text: The PyThrust repository was created on 2026-05-26T08:20:07Z.
PyThrust forks dated 2026-06-03 to 2026-10-01 include 7 on 2026-06-03 and 2 in August.
sentences.note: Source 312 lists 7 forks on 2026-06-03, 2 in August (08-23, 08-27), range 06-03 to 10-01.

sentences.text: mavlink2grpc was created on 2026-06-06 and had 2 releases on 2026-06-07.
sentences.note: Created 2026-06-06 per source 24; 2 releases on 2026-06-07 per source 320.

sentences.text: mavlink2grpc received 4 pull requests on 2026-06-07, all from people outside the owning organization.
sentences.note: Source 319 shows 4 PRs on 2026-06-07, all by outsiders.

sentences.text: mavlink2grpc was last pushed on 2026-06-18.
Studio was created on 2026-08-15 and had releases on 2026-08-29, 2026-08-29 and 2026-09-16.
sentences.note: Creation 2026-08-15 in source 65; three release dates match source 326.

sentences.text: Studio's pull requests page shows 45 pull requests dated 2026-08-27 to 2026-10-28, all by people outside the owning organization.
sentences.note: Source 325 states 45 PRs, 2026-08-27 to 2026-10-28, all 45 by outsiders.

sentences.text: Studio was last pushed on 2026-10-28.
PyThrust received 1 star event on 2026-10-12 and Studio received 1 on 2026-10-28.
sentences.note: Source 317 shows 1 star event on 2026-10-12; source 331 shows 1 on 2026-10-28.

sentences.text: The evidence shows open-source developer tools and no commercial product, so the path to revenue is unclear.
Studio has only 4 stars as of 2026-11-02 despite many pull requests, which may mean the outside pull requests are not a sign of real adoption.
mavlink2grpc has had no push since 2026-06-18, which may signal it is no longer a priority.
Defense positioning is not backed by anything in the public record.
The public record does not say who the founders are or what their backgrounds are.
It does not say how the company plans to earn revenue from open-source tools.
It does not show whether any user is a defense customer or whether the models were validated on hardware.
It does not explain who the outside pull request authors are or why Studio drew so many.

founder_call_questions: Who is on the team, and what is each person's background in UAVs or defense?
How do you plan to make money from open-source tools: hosted service, support, or a closed product?
Which defense or commercial customers use PyThrust, Studio or mavlink2grpc today?
How have PyThrust's motor, propeller and battery models been validated against bench or flight test data?
How does PyThrust compare in accuracy and speed with existing propulsion tools?
Who wrote the 45 outside pull requests on Studio, and were they solicited, for example through a program or a class?
What is the plugin strategy for Studio, and who are the early plugin authors?
Why has mavlink2grpc had no push since 2026-06-18, and is it still supported?
What is the product that ties the three repositories together?
What defense-specific needs, such as export control or secure deployment, shape the roadmap?
